messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 55-year-old married man of Ghanaian descent who has spent the better part of three decades as a bomb disposal technician, a profession that has always demanded that he hold chaos at arm's length through discipline, procedure, and an almost preternatural calm. That professional identity makes what happened to him three years ago feel, in his own words, like a particular kind of betrayal — not by an enemy or a device, but by the earth itself.

In the late summer of 2021, Kofi was visiting extended family in a coastal region of West Africa when a powerful tropical storm made landfall with almost no warning. The meteorological services had tracked the system, but its rapid intensification in the final hours meant that the community had perhaps forty minutes between the first serious alerts and the storm's arrival. Kofi was in his uncle's concrete-block house when the roof of the adjacent structure — a neighbour's home where children had been playing — collapsed under the combined force of wind and flooding. The noise was enormous and immediate: a percussive crack followed by a sustained roar that he has since described as the sound of everything solid becoming unreliable. He worked alongside neighbours to pull people from the debris for hours, in darkness, in water, amid the continuing violence of the wind. He does not know, even now, the full sequence of what he saw and did during those hours. The gaps in his recall are not modest. Significant stretches are simply absent, and what does surface comes in fragments — a child's sandal, a particular quality of grey light at dawn, the feeling of his hands on rubble — without narrative continuity to hold them together. When those fragments do surface, what accompanies them is not grief or fear but a white-hot rage that he finds almost impossible to account for and deeply disturbing to experience.

In the months after he returned to the United States, Kofi noticed that his body had begun operating on a logic he did not recognise. A car backfiring in the street near his home in suburban Maryland would send his heart into his throat and his muscles into a defensive crouch before he had consciously registered the sound. Colleagues raising their voices during a briefing — even in ordinary frustration, not directed at him — produced the same flooding physical response. He had come to understand intellectually that nothing was wrong in these moments, but the understanding arrived after the alarm, never before it, and the gap between the two felt humiliating to a man whose professional competence depended on his nervous system being an instrument of precision. Situations that resisted prediction — a change to a work schedule, an unplanned social event, any context where he could not know what was coming — produced a sustained, grinding vigilance that left him exhausted by midday.

What formed gradually, across weeks and then months, was a set of habits organised around reducing the possibility of being caught off guard. Kofi began declining any assignment that involved ambiguity about the operational environment, a pattern his supervisors initially accommodated but which has increasingly limited his deployment eligibility. He stopped attending the monthly team gatherings he had previously valued. At home, he keeps the television or a podcast running at virtually all hours — not to watch or listen, but because silence, he has found, leaves too much room. He eats heavily in the evenings, working through food in a way that his wife, Adwoa, has watched with quiet alarm, and which he knows is connected to the distress he cannot otherwise discharge. Adwoa has said, carefully and more than once, that she feels she is living with someone who is always waiting for the next disaster. He has not been able to tell her she is wrong.

What finally brought Kofi to the clinic was a near-miss at work six weeks ago: a moment of sensory overload during a training exercise that produced a flashback so complete that for several seconds he was not in Maryland but in the dark water of that night, hands on rubble, the roar still present. A colleague noticed and covered for him. Kofi drove home afterwards and sat in his car for an hour. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that he is becoming unreliable — in the field, and to his wife. What he hopes for, more tentatively, is to remember what happened without the rage, and to trust his own body again.
